content.title: About
content.content: Cooked tomatoes are the fruits of the tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum) that have been boiled until tender. Heat treatment retains most of their vitamins and minerals while making them easier to digest. They are used in sauces, soups, stews, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes belong to the nightshade family and are botanically classified as berries with juicy flesh.
Cooking increases the bioavailability of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Cooked tomatoes are a staple in many world cuisines, from Italian marinara to Russian shchi.
They contain about 90 % water, making them a low‑calorie food.
Tomatoes can be grown in greenhouses, allowing year‑round production.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a strong antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Cooked tomatoes retain a good amount of vitamin C, which boosts immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports proper heart function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to tomatoes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tomatoes can aggravate heartburn in individuals with high stomach acidity.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic tomatoes, rinse them thoroughly to reduce any pesticide residue.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked tomatoes can be added to sauces, soups, stews, pizza, casseroles, and salads. They are also used as purees or as the base for tomato paste. Serve them warm or chilled.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tomatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portion‑size bags—they will retain flavor and nutrients.
